title: Πάλη καὶ δρόμος
about: Achilles sets out prizes for the wrestling: a great tripod for the winner and a skilled woman for the loser. Telamonian Ajax and Odysseus grip each other and neither can throw the other; Ajax proposes that each lift the other, and in the lifting Odysseus trips him with a blow to the back of the knee, then fails to lift Ajax in his turn, and both fall. Achilles stops the bout and declares it a draw, with equal prizes. Next he sets a silver Sidonian mixing-bowl for the foot-race, with an ox and half a talent of gold behind it. Swift Ajax, son of Oileus, Odysseus and Antilochus run; Odysseus stays at Ajax’s heels and prays to Athena, who lightens his limbs and trips Ajax in the dung of the sacrificed cattle. Odysseus takes the bowl, Ajax the ox, and Antilochus, with a graceful compliment to Achilles, the gold, to which Achilles adds a second half-talent.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ αἶψ’ ἄλλα κατὰ τρίτα θῆκεν ἄεθλα
δεικνύμενος Δαναοῖσι παλαισμοσύνης ἀλεγεινῆς,
τῷ μὲν νικήσαντι μέγαν τρίποδ’ ἐμπυριβήτην,
τὸν δὲ δυωδεκάβοιον ἐνὶ σφίσι τῖον Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.l:
Peleus’-son at once set other contest-prizes, third in order,
displaying to the Danaans, for grievous wrestling:
to the winner a great fire-treading tripod,
and this, worth twelve oxen, among themselves the Achaeans valued;
sentences.i: The son of Peleus at once set out a further, third group of prizes, displaying to the Danaans what grievous wrestling would win: for the winner a great tripod to stand on the fire, which the Achaeans among themselves valued at twelve oxen;
sentences.n: The wrestling is the third event of the games for Patroclus. Πηλεΐδης is Achilles, ‘son of Peleus’, and ἄλλα κατὰ τρίτα means ‘other prizes, third in order’. δεικνύμενος ‘displaying’ governs Δαναοῖσι, and παλαισμοσύνης ἀλεγεινῆς is the genitive of the contest the prizes are for, ‘grievous wrestling’. ἐμπυριβήτην is ‘fire-treading’, from ἐν πυρί and βαίνω: a tripod made to stand over a fire. τῖον is the imperfect of τίω ‘value’, and the value is reckoned in oxen: δυωδεκάβοιον ‘worth twelve oxen’.

sentences.t:
ἀνδρὶ δὲ νικηθέντι γυναῖκ’ ἐς μέσσον ἔθηκε,
πολλὰ δ’ ἐπίστατο ἔργα, τίον δέ ἑ τεσσαράβοιον.
sentences.l:
And for the man defeated a woman into the midst he set,
many works she knew, and they valued her at four oxen.
sentences.i: For the man who was beaten he put a woman in the middle, one skilled in many kinds of work, and they valued her at four oxen.
sentences.n: The loser’s prize is a woman, put ἐς μέσσον ‘into the middle’ where all can see. Like the tripod she is given a price: τίον δέ ἑ τεσσαράβοιον ‘they valued her at four oxen’. πολλὰ … ἔργα ἐπίστατο is ‘she knew many works’, that is, many crafts. ἐπίστατο is the imperfect of ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how’, and ἑ is the epic ‘her’.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: Achilles is the subject (Πηλεΐδης, 700), and the line repeats at 752, where he calls the runners. στῆ is the aorist of ἵστημι ‘stand’, here intransitive, and ὀρθός ‘upright’. μῦθον ἔειπεν ‘spoke a word’ is a formula, with ἔειπεν the epic aorist of εἶπον. The colon opens his call in the next line.

sentences.t: ὄρνυσθ’ οἳ καὶ τούτου ἀέθλου πειρήσεσθον.
sentences.l: “Rise, you who of this contest also will make trial, you two.”
sentences.i: “Rise, you two who will try your strength in this contest also.”
sentences.n: ὄρνυσθ’ is the plural imperative ‘rouse yourselves, rise’, but πειρήσεσθον is the dual future, ‘you two will make trial’: Achilles calls to all and speaks of the pair who will wrestle. πειράομαι takes the genitive (ἀέθλου), ‘make trial of’. καί ‘also’ looks back to the chariot-race and the boxing already run.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δ’ ἔπειτα μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας,
ἂν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς πολύμητις ἀνίστατο κέρδεα εἰδώς.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and rose then great Telamonian Ajax,
and up many-wiled Odysseus stood, knowing cunning ways.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and great Telamonian Ajax rose, and up stood Odysseus of many wiles, knowing cunning ways.
sentences.n: This Ajax is Telamon’s son, ‘Telamonian’, the greater Ajax; the epithet tells him from the other Ajax, son of Oileus, who runs at 754. ὦρτο is the aorist of ὄρνυμι in the middle, ‘rose’. In ἂν δ’ … ἀνίστατο the preposition is split from its verb (tmesis), ‘up … stood’. πολύμητις ‘of many wiles’ and κέρδεα εἰδώς ‘knowing cunning ways’ are Odysseus’ stock phrases and are translated each time.

sentences.t:
ζωσαμένω δ’ ἄρα τώ γε βάτην ἐς μέσσον ἀγῶνα,
ἀγκὰς δ’ ἀλλήλων λαβέτην χερσὶ στιβαρῇσιν
ὡς ὅτ’ ἀμείβοντες, τούς τε κλυτὸς ἤραρε τέκτων
δώματος ὑψηλοῖο βίας ἀνέμων ἀλεείνων.
sentences.l:
And girded, the two then went into the middle of the gathering,
and in a clasp each other they took hold of with stout hands,
like rafters, which a famous builder has fitted
of a high house, shunning the force of the winds.
sentences.i: The two girded themselves and went into the middle of the gathering, and took hold of each other in a clasp with their stout hands, like the rafters that a famous builder has fitted to a high house, shunning the force of the winds.
sentences.n: ζωσαμένω … τώ γε βάτην are dual forms, ‘the two, having girded themselves, went’, and λαβέτην is a dual too; ἀγκάς ‘in the arms’ with ἀλλήλων ‘each other’. The simile compares the locked pair to ἀμείβοντες, taken to be the rafters of a roof, which lean against each other at the top; the sense is the traditional one. κλυτὸς … τέκτων is ‘a famous builder’, and the last line also stands at 16.213, in the simile of a man fitting a wall, where ἀλεείνων ‘shunning’ goes with him.

sentences.t:
τετρίγει δ’ ἄρα νῶτα θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
ἑλκόμενα στερεῶς·
sentences.l:
And creaked then the backs, from bold hands
dragged firmly;
sentences.i: Their backs creaked as the bold hands dragged them firmly;
sentences.n: The backs are the wrestlers’; the hands that pull them are the other man’s. τετρίγει is from τρίζω ‘creak, squeak’, in a perfect-stem form with the force of a simple past. θρασειάων is the epic feminine genitive plural of θρασύς ‘bold’, agreeing with χειρῶν. ἑλκόμενα ‘dragged’ agrees with νῶτα, and στερεῶς is ‘firmly’.

sentences.t:
κατὰ δὲ νότιος ῥέεν ἱδρώς,
πυκναὶ δὲ σμώδιγγες ἀνὰ πλευράς τε καὶ ὤμους
αἵματι φοινικόεσσαι ἀνέδραμον·
sentences.i: wet sweat ran down, and close-set weals, crimson with blood, sprang up along their ribs and shoulders;
sentences.n: The first half of the line sits in tmesis: κατὰ … ῥέεν ‘ran down’. νότιος ῥέεν ἱδρώς is ‘wet sweat’ (as at 11.811); νότιος is ‘moist’, not ‘southern’. σμώδιγγες are weals raised by the hard gripping, and φοινικόεσσαι ‘crimson’ is the feminine plural agreeing with them. ἀνέδραμον is the aorist of ἀνατρέχω ‘run up’, so the weals ‘ran up’ over the skin.

sentences.t:
οἳ δὲ μάλ’ αἰεὶ
νίκης ἱέσθην τρίποδος πέρι ποιητοῖο·
sentences.l:
but they, very much and ever,
were straining for victory, for the wrought tripod;
sentences.i: but they kept straining with all their might for victory, for the sake of the wrought tripod;
sentences.n: ἱέσθην is the dual of ἵεμαι ‘strain after’, with the genitive νίκης ‘for victory’; the same verb returns at 767 in the participle ἱεμένῳ. μάλ’ αἰεί ‘very much, always’. πέρι with the genitive means ‘for the sake of’, and ποιητοῖο ‘wrought’ (from ποιέω) is said of the tripod, the prize named at 702.

sentences.t:
οὔτ’ Ὀδυσεὺς δύνατο σφῆλαι οὔδει τε πελάσσαι,
οὔτ’ Αἴας δύνατο, κρατερὴ δ’ ἔχεν ἲς Ὀδυσῆος.
sentences.l:
Neither could Odysseus trip him and bring him to the ground,
nor could Ajax; and strong held the force of Odysseus.
sentences.i: Odysseus could not trip him and bring him to the ground, nor could Ajax do it to him; the strong force of Odysseus held fast.
sentences.n: δύνατο is the imperfect of δύναμαι, without the augment. σφῆλαι is the aorist infinitive of σφάλλω ‘trip up, make fall’, and πελάσσαι ‘bring near’ is used with οὔδει ‘to the ground’; the object ‘him’ is understood. In the second clause ἔχεν ‘held’ has no object, and is meant to say that Odysseus’ strength held firm. κρατερή ‘strong’ goes with ἲς ‘force’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἀνίαζον ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς,
δὴ τότε μιν προσέειπε μέγας Τελαμώνιος Αἴας·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they were wearying the well-greaved Achaeans,
then to him spoke great Telamonian Ajax:
sentences.i: But when the two were wearying the well-greaved Achaeans, then great Telamonian Ajax spoke to him:
sentences.n: The bout is a stalemate, and the onlookers tire of it. ἀνίαζον is the imperfect of ἀνιάζω ‘distress, weary’; the unnamed subject is the wrestling pair and the object is ἐϋκνήμιδας Ἀχαιούς, ‘well-greaved Achaeans’, the stock epithet. δὴ τότε ‘then at last’, and μιν is Odysseus. Ajax speaks first, in the next line.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ
ἤ μ’ ἀνάειρ’, ἢ ἐγὼ σέ·
sentences.l:
“Zeus-sprung son of Laertes, many-devising Odysseus,
either lift me, or I you;
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, either lift me, or let me lift you;
sentences.n: The first line is the address used at 2.173 and elsewhere: διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’, πολυμήχαν’ ‘many-devising’ (vocative, with Ὀδυσσεῦ). ἀνάειρ’ is the imperative of ἀναείρω ‘lift up’, and ἤ … ἢ is ‘either … or’. In ἢ ἐγὼ σέ the verb is left out, ‘or I (lift) you’.

sentences.t: τὰ δ’ αὖ Διὶ πάντα μελήσει.
sentences.l: and these things, in turn, to Zeus will all be a care.”
sentences.i: and the rest will be Zeus’s concern.”
sentences.n: τά is ‘these things’, meaning the outcome of the match. μελήσει is the future of μέλω, ‘will be a care to’, with the dative Διί. αὖ ‘in turn’ answers the earlier ‘lift me, or I you’: whichever of them lifts, the rest is for the god.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν ἀνάειρε· δόλου δ’ οὐ λήθετ’ Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he lifted him; and of the trick did not forget Odysseus;
sentences.i: With these words he lifted him; but Odysseus did not forget his trick:
sentences.n: εἰπών ‘having spoken’ is aorist, and ἀνάειρε ‘lifted’ is the verb Ajax has just used of himself. λήθετ’ is the unaugmented aorist of the middle λανθάνομαι ‘forget’, which takes the genitive δόλου ‘a trick’. The sentence continues in the next line with what the trick is.

sentences.t:
κόψ’ ὄπιθεν κώληπα τυχών, ὑπέλυσε δὲ γυῖα,
κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλ’ ἐξοπίσω·
sentences.l:
he struck from behind, having hit the knee-hollow, and loosened his limbs,
and down threw him backwards;
sentences.i: he struck him from behind, hitting the back of the knee, and loosened his limbs from under him, and threw him down on his back;
sentences.n: κόψ’ is the aorist of κόπτω ‘strike’; ὄπιθεν ‘from behind’. τυχών ‘having hit’ is the aorist participle of τυγχάνω, taking κώληπα, the hollow at the back of the knee. ὑπέλυσε δὲ γυῖα is ‘loosened his limbs from under him’ (ὑπο- ‘beneath’). In κὰδ … ἔβαλ’ ἐξοπίσω the preposition is split off (tmesis): ‘threw down backwards’.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ στήθεσσιν Ὀδυσσεὺς
κάππεσε·
sentences.l:
and on his chest Odysseus
fell;
sentences.i: and Odysseus fell upon his chest;
sentences.n: Ajax goes over backwards, and Odysseus falls on top of him. κάππεσε is κατέπεσε (the κατ- assimilated to the π), the aorist of καταπίπτω ‘fall’. στήθεσσιν is the epic dative plural ‘chest’, with ἐπί ‘upon’.

sentences.t: λαοὶ δ’ αὖ θηεῦντό τε θάμβησάν τε.
sentences.l: and the people in turn both gazed and were struck with wonder.
sentences.i: and the people gazed, and were struck with wonder.
sentences.n: θηεῦντο is the epic imperfect of θηέομαι ‘gaze at’, and θάμβησαν the aorist of θαμβέω ‘be struck with wonder’; τε … τε ties the two verbs together. αὖ ‘in turn’ marks the crowd’s reaction after the fall.

sentences.t:
δεύτερος αὖτ’ ἀνάειρε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
κίνησεν δ’ ἄρα τυτθὸν ἀπὸ χθονός, οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ἄειρεν,
ἐν δὲ γόνυ γνάμψεν·
sentences.i: Then, taking the second turn, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus lifted him; he moved him a little off the ground but could lift him no higher, and a knee was bent in;
sentences.n: δεύτερος αὖτ’ is ‘second, in his turn’: Ajax’s first lift was answered by a lift from Odysseus. πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is his name-formula, ‘much-enduring, heavenly’. κίνησεν is ‘moved’, and τυτθόν ‘a little’. The last verb has no named subject: ἐν δὲ γόνυ γνάμψεν is ‘and bent a knee in’, and the natural reading is that Ajax hooks his knee into Odysseus’ and so brings him down; ἐν is an adverb (‘in’).

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δὲ χθονὶ κάππεσον ἄμφω
πλησίοι ἀλλήλοισι, μιάνθησαν δὲ κονίῃ.
sentences.l:
and on the earth fell both
near each other, and were stained with dust.
sentences.i: and both fell to the ground close to each other, and were stained with dust.
sentences.n: So the second fall ends in a tie. κάππεσον is the plural of κάππεσε at 728 (‘fell’), now with ἄμφω ‘both’. πλησίοι is the epic ‘near’, with the dative ἀλλήλοισι ‘each other’. μιάνθησαν is the aorist passive of μιαίνω, ‘were stained’, with the dative κονίῃ ‘with dust’.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κε τὸ τρίτον αὖτις ἀναΐξαντ’ ἐπάλαιον,
εἰ μὴ Ἀχιλλεὺς αὐτὸς ἀνίστατο καὶ κατέρυκε·
sentences.l:
And now the third time again, having sprung up, they would have wrestled,
if Achilles himself had not stood up and held them back:
sentences.i: And they would have wrestled a third time, springing up again, if Achilles himself had not stood up and held them back:
sentences.n: καί νύ κε with the imperfect ἐπάλαιον is an unreal past, ‘they would have wrestled’, and εἰ μὴ … ἀνίστατο καὶ κατέρυκε gives the condition that did not happen. ἀναΐξαντ’ is the dual aorist participle ‘having sprung up’ (ἀναΐσσω); τὸ τρίτον ‘the third time’. κατέρυκε is the imperfect of κατερύκω ‘hold back, restrain’. Achilles’ words follow.

sentences.t: μηκέτ’ ἐρείδεσθον, μὴ δὲ τρίβεσθε κακοῖσι·
sentences.l: “No longer press on, and do not wear yourselves out with ills;
sentences.i: “No longer press on, and do not wear yourselves out with hardships;
sentences.n: Another change of number: ἐρείδεσθον is the dual imperative (‘you two’) of ἐρείδω ‘press, lean hard’ in the middle, and τρίβεσθε is the plural imperative of τρίβω ‘wear down’. μὴ δέ is two words, ‘and not’. κακοῖσι is ‘with ills, with hardships’, the dative of means. Achilles stops the bout as a draw.

sentences.t:
νίκη δ’ ἀμφοτέροισιν· ἀέθλια δ’ ἶσ’ ἀνελόντες
ἔρχεσθ’, ὄφρα καὶ ἄλλοι ἀεθλεύωσιν Ἀχαιοί.
sentences.l:
victory is for both; and equal contest-prizes having taken up,
go, so that others also may contend, Achaeans.”
sentences.i: the victory is for both; take equal prizes and go, so that other Achaeans may contend as well.”
sentences.n: νίκη ἀμφοτέροισιν has no verb, ‘victory (is) for both’. ἀέθλια are ‘contest-prizes’, and ἶσ’ is ἴσα ‘equal’; ἀνελόντες is the aorist participle of ἀναιρέω ‘take up’. ἔρχεσθ’ is ‘go’ (imperative), and ὄφρα with the subjunctive ἀεθλεύωσιν gives the purpose: ‘so that they may contend’. The Achaeans are the others, not the pair, and the speech ends.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδὲ πίθοντο,
καί ῥ’ ἀπομορξαμένω κονίην δύσαντο χιτῶνας.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed,
and, having wiped off the dust, put on their tunics.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed, and wiped off the dust and put on their tunics.
sentences.n: The first line is also 9.79 (there with a full stop), the stock sense ‘heard and obeyed’. οἳ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’; τοῦ is the article as a pronoun, ‘him’, with the genitive after κλύον. ἀπομορξαμένω is a dual aorist participle ‘having wiped off’, and δύσαντο the aorist middle of δύω, ‘put on’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ αἶψ’ ἄλλα τίθει ταχυτῆτος ἄεθλα
ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα τετυγμένον·
sentences.l:
Peleus’-son at once set other contest-prizes for speed,
a silver mixing-bowl, wrought;
sentences.i: Then at once the son of Peleus set out other prizes, for a race: a silver mixing-bowl, well-wrought;
sentences.n: ταχυτῆτος is the genitive of ταχυτής ‘speed’, so the contest is the foot-race; ἄεθλα is ‘contest-prizes’. τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι ‘was setting out’. The first prize is an ἀργύρεον κρητῆρα, a silver mixing-bowl for wine and water, and τετυγμένον is the perfect participle of τεύχω ‘made, wrought’.

sentences.t:
ἓξ δ’ ἄρα μέτρα
χάνδανεν, αὐτὰρ κάλλει ἐνίκα πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν
πολλόν, ἐπεὶ Σιδόνες πολυδαίδαλοι εὖ ἤσκησαν,
sentences.l:
and six measures
it held, and in beauty it surpassed over all the earth
by far, since the Sidonians, skilled in much intricate work, had worked it well,
sentences.i: It held six measures, and for beauty it surpassed every other on all the earth by far, because the Sidonians, so skilled in intricate work, had worked it well;
sentences.n: χάνδανεν is the imperfect of χανδάνω ‘hold, contain’, and μέτρα are ‘measures’; the word does not say how large. κάλλει ἐνίκα … πολλόν is ‘it won in beauty by much’, and the thing it beat is the other bowls ‘over all the earth’ (πᾶσαν ἐπ’ αἶαν). Σιδόνες are the craftsmen of Sidon. πολυδαίδαλοι is the word used of things as ‘much-wrought’; said of men it means ‘skilled in much intricate work’. ἤσκησαν is the aorist of ἀσκέω ‘work, fashion’.

sentences.t:
Φοίνικες δ’ ἄγον ἄνδρες ἐπ’ ἠεροειδέα πόντον,
στῆσαν δ’ ἐν λιμένεσσι, Θόαντι δὲ δῶρον ἔδωκαν·
sentences.l:
and Phoenician men carried it over the misty-looking sea,
and made stand in harbours, and to Thoas as a gift they gave it;
sentences.i: and Phoenician men carried it over the misty-looking sea and moored in harbours, and gave it to Thoas as a gift;
sentences.n: Φοίνικες … ἄνδρες is ‘Phoenician men’, the sea-traders, and ἠεροειδέα is a stock epithet of the sea, ‘misty-looking’ (ἀήρ ‘mist’ + εἶδος). στῆσαν is the transitive aorist of ἵστημι ‘made stand’; its object is not stated, and what is meant is that they brought the ship to rest. Θόαντι is the dative of Thoas, to whom they gave δῶρον ‘a gift’.

sentences.t:
υἷος δὲ Πριάμοιο Λυκάονος ὦνον ἔδωκε
Πατρόκλῳ ἥρωϊ Ἰησονίδης Εὔνηος.
sentences.l:
and for the son of Priam, Lycaon, the price he gave
to the hero Patroclus, Jason’s-son Euneus.
sentences.i: and Euneus, son of Jason, gave it to the hero Patroclus as the price for Lycaon, son of Priam.
sentences.n: The subject is at the end of the sentence: Ἰησονίδης Εὔνηος, ‘Euneus, Jason’s son’. ὦνον is ‘price’, and υἷος … Πριάμοιο Λυκάονος in the genitive says what it was the price of, ‘the son of Priam, Lycaon’; so Euneus paid the bowl to Patroclus as the price for Lycaon. The Greek does not say here how Lycaon came to be sold. ἔδωκε is ‘gave’, and ἥρωϊ is ‘to the hero’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸν Ἀχιλλεὺς θῆκεν ἄεθλον οὗ ἑτάροιο,
ὅς τις ἐλαφρότατος ποσσὶ κραιπνοῖσι πέλοιτο·
sentences.l:
And this Achilles set as a contest-prize of his own companion,
whoever should be lightest on rushing feet;
sentences.i: Achilles set it out as a prize for his own companion’s games, for whoever should prove the lightest on his rushing feet;
sentences.n: καὶ τόν ‘and this one’ is the bowl. οὗ ἑτάροιο is the genitive ‘of his own companion’ (οὗ is the possessive ‘his own’, not the relative), Patroclus, whose funeral the games honour. ὅς τις … πέλοιτο is ‘whoever should be’, with the optative of a general condition. ἐλαφρότατος is ‘lightest’, and κραιπνοῖσι ‘rushing’ is the epithet of feet seen at 6.505.

sentences.t:
δευτέρῳ αὖ βοῦν θῆκε μέγαν καὶ πίονα δημῷ,
ἡμιτάλαντον δὲ χρυσοῦ λοισθήϊ’ ἔθηκε.
sentences.l:
For the second, in turn, an ox he set, great and fat with tallow,
and half a talent of gold as last prize he set.
sentences.i: For the second he set a great ox, fat with tallow, and for the last he set half a talent of gold.
sentences.n: δευτέρῳ ‘for the second (runner)’ is dative; αὖ ‘in turn’ continues the list of prizes. πίονα δημῷ is ‘fat with tallow’, with the dative of respect. ἡμιτάλαντον is ‘a half-talent’, a weight of gold, and λοισθήϊ’ is the neuter plural ‘as the last prize(s)’. The third prize is the lowest.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ὀρθὸς καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: and he stood upright and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: He stood up straight and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: The same line as 706, for the same man, Achilles, now calling for runners. The colon leads into the speech in the next line.

sentences.t: ὄρνυσθ’ οἳ καὶ τούτου ἀέθλου πειρήσεσθε.
sentences.l: “Rise, you who of this contest also will make trial.”
sentences.i: “Rise, you who will try your strength in this contest also.”
sentences.n: As at 707, but with the plural πειρήσεσθε ‘you will make trial of’: this contest takes many runners, not a pair. ὄρνυσθ’ is the imperative ‘rouse yourselves’, and τούτου ἀέθλου the genitive after πειράομαι.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, ὄρνυτο δ’ αὐτίκ’ Ὀϊλῆος ταχὺς Αἴας,
ἂν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς πολύμητις, ἔπειτα δὲ Νέστορος υἱὸς
Ἀντίλοχος·
sentences.i: So he spoke, and swift Ajax, son of Oileus, started up at once, and Odysseus of many wiles, and after them Nestor’s son Antilochus;
sentences.n: Here Ajax is the son of Oileus (Ὀϊλῆος), the ‘swift’ Ajax, not the Telamonian of the wrestling. ὄρνυτο is the middle ‘rose’, and ἂν δ’ … is the same split ‘up’ (tmesis) as at 709, with the verb carried over. Νέστορος υἱός ‘Nestor’s son’ is Antilochus, the young runner of 756.

sentences.t: ὃ γὰρ αὖτε νέους ποσὶ πάντας ἐνίκα.
sentences.l: for he, in turn, all the young men with his feet surpassed.
sentences.i: for he, in his turn, beat all the young men in speed.
sentences.n: ὃ γάρ gives the reason: ὅ is the article as a pronoun, ‘he’, Antilochus. νέους … πάντας is ‘all the young men’, ποσί ‘with his feet’ (in running), and ἐνίκα the imperfect ‘was surpassing’. αὖτε ‘in his turn’ is the poet’s aside on the young runner.

sentences.t: στὰν δὲ μεταστοιχί· σήμηνε δὲ τέρματ’ Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.l: They stood in a line; and Achilles marked the limits.
sentences.i: They stood in a line, and Achilles marked out the limits of the course.
sentences.n: στὰν is ἔσταν, the intransitive aorist of ἵστημι, ‘they stood’, and μεταστοιχί is ‘in a row’. σήμηνε is ‘marked’, and τέρματα are ‘limits’, the marks that bound the course.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δ’ ἀπὸ νύσσης τέτατο δρόμος·
sentences.l: and for them from the starting-post the course was stretched;
sentences.i: From the starting-post the course was stretched out before them;
sentences.n: τέτατο is the pluperfect passive of τείνω ‘stretch’, so ‘was stretched out’. νύσσα is a post or mark on the course; here it is the one from which they start. δρόμος is ‘the course’, the running itself.

sentences.t:
ὦκα δ’ ἔπειτα
ἔκφερ’ Ὀϊλιάδης·
sentences.l:
and swiftly then
bore ahead Oileus’-son;
sentences.i: and then Oileus’ son swiftly forged ahead;
sentences.n: ὦκα ‘swiftly’ goes with ἔκφερ’, the imperfect of ἐκφέρω, which here means ‘bore out in front’, that is, took the lead (at 785 it means ‘carried off’ a prize). Ὀϊλιάδης is the patronymic of Ajax, son of Oileus.

sentences.t:
ἐπὶ δ’ ὄρνυτο δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἄγχι μάλ’, ὡς ὅτε τίς τε γυναικὸς ἐϋζώνοιο
στήθεός ἐστι κανών, ὅν τ’ εὖ μάλα χερσὶ τανύσσῃ
πηνίον ἐξέλκουσα παρὲκ μίτον,
sentences.l:
and close after rose heavenly Odysseus
very near, as when of a well-girdled woman
the breast’s rod is, which very well with her hands she stretches,
drawing out the spool past the thread,
sentences.i: Heavenly Odysseus rose to run after him, very near, as near as the rod is to the breast of a well-girdled woman when she draws it taut in her hands as she pulls the spool out past the thread,
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … ὄρνυτο is ‘rose after’. ἄγχι μάλ’ is ‘very near’, and the simile ὡς ὅτε … answers it with ὣς in 763. ἐϋζώνοιο ‘well-girdled’ is the stock epithet of women. κανών is a rod, here one used in weaving; what exact part of the loom is not said. ὅν τ’ … τανύσσῃ is the subjunctive of τανύω ‘stretch taut’, and πηνίον ‘spool’ is what she draws out, ἐξέλκουσα, παρὲκ μίτον ‘past the thread’.

sentences.t:
ἀγχόθι δ’ ἴσχει
στήθεος·
sentences.l:
and near she holds it
to the breast;
sentences.i: and holds it close to her breast;
sentences.n: ἀγχόθι is ‘near’, and ἴσχει ‘holds’; στήθεος is the genitive after it, ‘near the breast’. The woman keeps the rod close in at her breast, and the close-up is the point of the simile.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς θέεν ἐγγύθεν, αὐτὰρ ὄπισθεν
ἴχνια τύπτε πόδεσσι πάρος κόνιν ἀμφιχυθῆναι·
sentences.l:
so Odysseus ran close, and behind
he trod the footprints with his feet before the dust was poured around them;
sentences.i: so Odysseus ran close, and behind him trod in his footprints before the dust could spread round them;
sentences.n: ὣς answers the ὡς ὅτε of 760. θέεν is the imperfect of θέω ‘run’. ἴχνια are ‘footprints’, those of the runner ahead, and τύπτε πόδεσσι is ‘struck with his feet’. πάρος … ἀμφιχυθῆναι is ‘before it was poured around’, the aorist passive infinitive of ἀμφιχέω, with κόνιν ‘dust’ as subject: his steps fall on the prints before the dust has spread round them.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἄρα οἱ κεφαλῆς χέ’ ἀϋτμένα δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
αἰεὶ ῥίμφα θέων·
sentences.l:
and down on his head poured his breath heavenly Odysseus,
always running nimbly;
sentences.i: and heavenly Odysseus, running always nimbly, poured his breath down on his head;
sentences.n: In κὰδ … χέ’ the preposition is split from the verb (tmesis), ‘poured down’; χέ’ is χέε, the unaugmented imperfect of χέω. οἱ κεφαλῆς is ‘on his head’ (the leader’s). ἀϋτμένα is the epic accusative of ἀϋτμήν ‘breath’. ῥίμφα is ‘nimbly’, and θέων ‘running’ is the participle of θέω.

sentences.t:
ἴαχον δ’ ἐπὶ πάντες Ἀχαιοὶ
νίκης ἱεμένῳ, μάλα δὲ σπεύδοντι κέλευον.
sentences.l:
and shouted thereupon all the Achaeans,
to him straining for victory, and hurrying hard they urged him on.
sentences.i: and all the Achaeans shouted, urging him on as he strained for victory and hurried hard.
sentences.n: ἴαχον is the imperfect of ἰάχω ‘cry out’, with ἐπί as an adverb, ‘thereupon, in addition’. νίκης ἱεμένῳ is dative, ‘to him straining for victory’ (the verb is that of 718), and the second dative, σπεύδοντι ‘hurrying’, belongs to the same man, Odysseus. κέλευον is ‘were urging’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πύματον τέλεον δρόμον, αὐτίκ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
εὔχετ’ Ἀθηναίῃ γλαυκώπιδι ὃν κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.l:
But when they were finishing the last stretch of the course, at once Odysseus
prayed to gleaming-eyed Athena in his own heart:
sentences.i: But when they were finishing the last stretch of the course, Odysseus at once prayed in his own heart to gleaming-eyed Athena:
sentences.n: τέλεον is the imperfect of τελέω ‘finish, complete’, with δρόμον πύματον ‘the last part of the course’. εὔχετ’ is the imperfect middle of εὔχομαι ‘pray’; the dative Ἀθηναίῃ γλαυκώπιδι is ‘to gleaming-eyed Athena’ (γλαυκῶπις, the stock epithet). ὃν κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in his own heart’, so the prayer is silent, and the words follow.

sentences.t: κλῦθι θεά, ἀγαθή μοι ἐπίρροθος ἐλθὲ ποδοῖιν.
sentences.l: “Hear, goddess; come as a good helper to my two feet.”
sentences.i: “Hear me, goddess, and come as a good helper to my feet.”
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’; ἐπίρροθος is ‘helper’ (in the Odyssey the word is used of Athena as helper at 4.390), ἀγαθή ‘good’ is feminine because the helper asked for is the goddess herself. ἐλθέ is the aorist imperative of ἔρχομαι, and ποδοῖιν is the dual dative ‘to my two feet’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος· τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη,
γυῖα δ’ ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρά, πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, praying, and Pallas Athena heard him,
and made his limbs light, his feet and his hands above.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him, and made his limbs light, his feet and his hands and the limbs above them.
sentences.n: Both lines are the ones that answer Diomedes’ prayer to Athena at 5.121–122: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, praying’, then the god. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is the god’s name-formula. ἔθηκεν ἐλαφρά is ‘made light’; πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν is ‘his feet and his hands above’, taken to mean the upper limbs above the feet.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τάχ’ ἔμελλον ἐπαΐξασθαι ἄεθλον,
ἔνθ’ Αἴας μὲν ὄλισθε θέων, βλάψεν γὰρ Ἀθήνη,
τῇ ῥα βοῶν κέχυτ’ ὄνθος ἀποκταμένων ἐριμύκων,
οὓς ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ πέφνεν πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they were about to dash on the contest-prize,
then Ajax slipped as he ran, for Athena harmed him,
where of cattle the dung had been spilled, of slain, loud-bellowing cattle,
which for Patroclus had slain swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: But just as they were about to dash for the prize, Ajax slipped as he ran — for Athena harmed him — where the dung of slaughtered, loud-bellowing cattle had been spilled, cattle that Achilles, swift of foot, had slain for Patroclus:
sentences.n: The Ajax who slips is the son of Oileus, the leader. ἔμελλον ἐπαΐξασθαι is ‘were about to dash upon’, and ἄεθλον is the prize. βλάψεν is the aorist of βλάπτω ‘harm, hinder’. τῇ ῥα is ‘where’. κέχυτ’ is the pluperfect passive of χέω, ‘had been spilled’, and ἀποκταμένων ‘slain’. ἐριμύκων is ‘loud-bellowing’, and ἐπὶ Πατρόκλῳ is ‘for Patroclus’, the cattle killed at his funeral. πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς is a stock name-formula.

sentences.t: ἐν δ’ ὄνθου βοέου πλῆτο στόμα τε ῥῖνάς τε·
sentences.l: and with ox-dung he was filled, in mouth and nostrils;
sentences.i: and he was filled with ox-dung in mouth and nostrils;
sentences.n: ἐν … πλῆτο is the aorist of ἐμπίμπλημι ‘fill’ in the passive sense ‘was filled’, split by tmesis, and it takes the genitive ὄνθου βοέου ‘ox-dung’ (βοέου is ‘of an ox’). The unnamed subject is Ajax; στόμα ‘mouth’ and ῥῖνας ‘nostrils’ are both accusatives of the part affected (‘in mouth and nostrils’), and τε … τε links them.

sentences.t:
κρητῆρ’ αὖτ’ ἀνάειρε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ὡς ἦλθε φθάμενος·
sentences.l:
the mixing-bowl in turn lifted up much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
as he came, having got ahead;
sentences.i: Much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus took up the mixing-bowl, since he had come in first;
sentences.n: Odysseus takes the first prize, the silver bowl of 741. ἀνάειρε is ‘lifted up’ (as in the wrestling), κρητῆρ’ ‘mixing-bowl’, and αὖτ’ ‘in turn’. φθάμενος is the aorist middle participle of φθάνω ‘get ahead of’, so ‘having got in first’. ὡς can be ‘since’ or ‘when’; the sense is the same. The name-formula is πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.

sentences.t: ὃ δὲ βοῦν ἕλε φαίδιμος Αἴας.
sentences.l: and the ox took glorious Ajax.
sentences.i: and glorious Ajax took the ox.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, the other man, Ajax, who is named at the end. βοῦν is ‘the ox’, the second prize of 750, and ἕλε the aorist of αἱρέω ‘take’. φαίδιμος ‘glorious’ is the stock epithet, translated even here.

sentences.t:
στῆ δὲ κέρας μετὰ χερσὶν ἔχων βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο
ὄνθον ἀποπτύων, μετὰ δ’ Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
And he stood, the horn in his hands holding of the field-dwelling ox,
spitting out the dung, and among the Argives spoke:
sentences.i: He stood holding in his hands the horn of the ox of the fields, spitting out the dung, and spoke among the Argives:
sentences.n: Ajax stands there with his prize, ‘the horn of the ox’ in his hands. βοὸς ἀγραύλοιο is ‘of the field-dwelling ox’, ἀγραῦλος being formed from ἀγρός ‘field’ and probably αὐλή ‘dwelling’. ἀποπτύων is ‘spitting out’, with ὄνθον ‘dung’ as its object. μετὰ … ἔειπεν is ‘spoke among’.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἦ μ’ ἔβλαψε θεὰ πόδας, ἣ τὸ πάρος περ
μήτηρ ὣς Ὀδυσῆϊ παρίσταται ἠδ’ ἐπαρήγει.
sentences.l:
“Ah, truly the goddess harmed me in my feet, she who as before
like a mother stands by Odysseus and aids him.”
sentences.i: “Ah, it is the goddess who harmed my feet — she who, as ever before, stands by Odysseus like a mother and helps him.”
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is the exclamation ‘Ah’. ἦ is ‘truly’; ἔβλαψε is the aorist of βλάπτω ‘harm’ (as in 774), and πόδας is the accusative of the part hit, ‘in the feet’. θεά is Athena, not named. τὸ πάρος περ is ‘as before’. παρίσταται is ‘stands beside’, and ἐπαρήγει ‘helps’; ὣς with μήτηρ means ‘like a mother’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ἡδὺ γέλασσαν.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they all then sweetly laughed at him.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all laughed with relish at him.
sentences.n: The line has the same shape as 738. ἡδὺ γέλασσαν is ‘sweetly laughed’ (the adverb ἡδύ, ‘with relish’), the aorist of γελάω with ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘at him’. The laughter follows his complaint.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχος δ’ ἄρα δὴ λοισθήϊον ἔκφερ’ ἄεθλον
μειδιόων, καὶ μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
And Antilochus then bore off the last contest-prize,
smiling, and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.i: Antilochus carried off the last prize, smiling, and spoke a word among the Argives:
sentences.n: λοισθήϊον ἄεθλον is ‘the last contest-prize’, the half-talent of 751. ἔκφερ’ is the imperfect of ἐκφέρω ‘carry off’ (at 759 it meant ‘bore out in front’). μειδιόων ‘smiling’ is the Homeric participle of μειδάω. μῦθον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἔειπεν is the formula of 706, and the speech follows.

sentences.t:
εἰδόσιν ὔμμ’ ἐρέω πᾶσιν φίλοι, ὡς ἔτι καὶ νῦν
ἀθάνατοι τιμῶσι παλαιοτέρους ἀνθρώπους.
sentences.l:
“To those who know, I shall tell you, friends, all of you, how still even now
the immortals honour older men.
sentences.i: “I shall tell you, friends, who all know it, how even now the immortals still honour men who are older.
sentences.n: εἰδόσιν … πᾶσιν is the dative plural of the participle of οἶδα, ‘to all of you who know’, with ὔμμ’ the epic accusative ‘you’ and ἐρέω ‘I shall tell’. ὡς here is ‘how’, ἔτι καὶ νῦν ‘still even now’. ἀθάνατοι are the gods, and παλαιοτέρους ἀνθρώπους ‘older men’ is the comparative of παλαιός. His point is the one he goes on to make about Odysseus.

sentences.t:
Αἴας μὲν γὰρ ἐμεῖ’ ὀλίγον προγενέστερός ἐστιν,
οὗτος δὲ προτέρης γενεῆς προτέρων τ’ ἀνθρώπων·
sentences.l:
for Ajax is a little older than I,
but this man is of an earlier generation, and of earlier men:
sentences.i: for Ajax is only a little older than I, but this man belongs to an earlier generation, to earlier men:
sentences.n: The Ajax is the son of Oileus, the runner who slipped. ἐμεῖ’ is ἐμεῖο, ‘than me’, the genitive of comparison, and προγενέστερος is ‘born earlier’, ‘older’. οὗτος is Odysseus, ‘this man’, and the genitives προτέρης γενεῆς προτέρων τ’ ἀνθρώπων say ‘of an earlier generation and of earlier men’. γάρ gives the reason for the claim about the gods.

sentences.t: ὠμογέροντα δέ μίν φασ’ ἔμμεναι·
sentences.l: and a green old man they say he is;
sentences.i: and they say he is an old man still in his strength;
sentences.n: ὠμογέροντα is the accusative of ὠμογέρων, from ὠμός ‘raw’ and γέρων ‘old man’, understood as an old man with a fresh, unspent vigour. φασ’ is φασί ‘they say’, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive ‘to be’; μίν is ‘him’, Odysseus.

sentences.t:
ἀργαλέον δὲ
ποσσὶν ἐριδήσασθαι Ἀχαιοῖς, εἰ μὴ Ἀχιλλεῖ.
sentences.l:
and it is hard
in feet to strive for Achaeans, if not for Achilles.”
sentences.i: and it is hard for any Achaean to strive with him on foot, except Achilles.”
sentences.n: ἀργαλέον ‘hard’ stands without a verb. ποσσὶν ἐριδήσασθαι is ‘to strive with the feet’, the aorist infinitive of ἐριδαίνομαι (‘quarrel’, here of a contest), and Ἀχαιοῖς is the dative of the person, ‘for Achaeans’; the opponent ‘him’ (Odysseus) is understood. εἰ μὴ Ἀχιλλεῖ ‘except for Achilles’ prepares for the compliment that Achilles answers.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, κύδηνεν δὲ ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and glorified the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and paid honour to the fleet-footed son of Peleus.
sentences.n: κύδηνεν is the aorist of κυδαίνω ‘glorify, exalt’, with ποδώκεα Πηλεΐωνα ‘the fleet-footed son of Peleus’, Achilles, as the object. ποδώκης ‘fleet-footed’ is the stock epithet; the exalting is the speech’s last words, that only Achilles can outrun Odysseus.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἀχιλεὺς μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l: And him Achilles with words, answering, addressed:
sentences.i: Achilles answered him and spoke in these words:
sentences.n: Ἀχιλεύς here has one λ (as against Ἀχιλλεύς at 757), a variant the metre allows. μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν is the reply-formula, ‘answering with words, spoke to’; τόν is the article as a pronoun, ‘him’, Antilochus.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίλοχ’ οὐ μέν τοι μέλεος εἰρήσεται αἶνος,
ἀλλά τοι ἡμιτάλαντον ἐγὼ χρυσοῦ ἐπιθήσω.
sentences.l:
“Antilochus, truly not idle will your praise be said,
but half a talent of gold I myself shall add for you.”
sentences.i: “Antilochus, your praise shall not be spoken idly; I myself shall add half a talent of gold for you.”
sentences.n: μέλεος is ‘idle, vain’, and εἰρήσεται, the future passive of ἐρέω ‘say’, gives ‘will be said’; οὐ μέν τοι is ‘truly not’. αἶνος ‘praise’ is what Antilochus has just given him. ἡμιτάλαντον … χρυσοῦ is ‘a half-talent of gold’, as in 751, and ἐπιθήσω ‘I shall add’ puts it on top of the prize he has already won.
